extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in law, free speech, and satire
extracted.subtask_description: A news report summarizing a legal dispute over satirical/parodic speech (The Onion's amicus brief and the Novak Facebook-parody case), including legal doctrines, risks to satirists, and procedural tactics for Supreme Court review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody warning requirement (as suggested by Sixth Circuit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sixth Circuit's decision 'suggests that parodists are in the clear only if they pop the balloon in advance by warning their audience that their parody is not true.' The decision would 'condition the First Amendment's protection for parody upon a requirement that parodists explicitly say, up-front, that their work is nothing more than an elaborate fiction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted from The Onion's amicus brief describing the appeals court's reasoning; implies that under that ruling a creator who does not make the satirical nature explicit could be vulnerable to prosecution or civil liability. The Onion argues this would imperil parody and is an unacceptable requirement for satirists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified immunity standard for law enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualified immunity is a legal doctrine that largely shields law enforcement officers from constitutional claims when officers reasonably believed they were acting within the bounds of the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Novak's case, the Sixth Circuit granted officers qualified immunity — barring his suit — because officers 'reasonably believed they were acting within the bounds of the law,' even though the panel criticized the officers' actions. This is a standard applied to evaluate officials' liability, not a commentary on whether actions were justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience perception of authenticity affects protection for parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a satirical or parodic work is perceived by the audience as real or as fiction influences legal treatment; courts may consider if the parody is likely to be understood as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The case facts (a fake Facebook page that looked nearly identical to an official police page, including fake job postings and inflammatory notifications) are used to show how close imitation can lead to ambiguity in audience perception, which in turn affects First Amendment analysis as described by courts and briefing parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of criminal or civil consequences when satire impersonates official entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating a satirical work that closely mimics an official government or police communication can expose the creator to criminal charges (e.g., disrupting public services) or civil suits if authorities interpret the imitation as harmful or deceptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Anthony Novak was arrested and charged with one felony count of disrupting public services after launching a Facebook page that mirrored the Parma, Ohio Police Department's official page; he was later acquitted at trial, but subsequent qualified immunity rulings blocked his civil suit. The article implies satirists should be cautious about indistinguishable impersonation of official sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of amicus briefs to highlight importance and assist certiorari chances
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing a friend-of-the-court (amicus) brief can help draw attention to a petition for Supreme Court review and underscore the broader importance of the legal issue presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steve Vladeck is quoted noting the Supreme Court receives over 5,000 cert petitions yearly and grants about one percent; thus, having an effective amicus brief (like The Onion's) 'can’t hurt' and may improve the visibility of a case when seeking certiorari.
